# elsa - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/elsa/1.11.2/elsa/index.html

## Expand description

*🎵 Immutability never bothered me anyway 🎶*

This crate provides various “Frozen” collections.

These are append-only collections where references to entries can be held
on to even across insertions. This is safe because these collections only
support storing data that’s present behind some indirection – i.e. `String`,
`Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, etc, and they only yield references to the data behind the
allocation (`&str`, `&[T]`, and `&T` respectively)

The typical use case is having a global cache of strings or other data which the rest of the program borrows from.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use map::`- [FrozenBTreeMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.FrozenBTreeMap.html);
- `pub use map::`- [FrozenMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.FrozenMap.html);
- `pub use vec::`- [FrozenVec](https://docs.rs/vec/struct.FrozenVec.html);
- `pub use index_map::`- [FrozenIndexMap](https://docs.rs/index_map/struct.FrozenIndexMap.html);
- `pub use index_set::`- [FrozenIndexSet](https://docs.rs/index_set/struct.FrozenIndexSet.html);

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/elsa/1.11.2/src/elsa/lib.rs.html

# elsa/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! _🎵 Immutability never bothered me anyway 🎶_
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate provides various "Frozen" collections.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! These are append-only collections where references to entries can be held
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! on to even across insertions. This is safe because these collections only
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! support storing data that's present behind some indirection -- i.e. `String`,
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, etc, and they only yield references to the data behind the
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! allocation (`&str`, `&[T]`, and `&T` respectively)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! The typical use case is having a global cache of strings or other data which the rest of the program borrows from.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)
[13](https://docs.rs#13)pub mod map;
[14](https://docs.rs#14)pub mod vec;
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)#[cfg(feature = "indexmap")]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)pub mod index_map;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)#[cfg(feature = "indexmap")]
[19](https://docs.rs#19)pub mod index_set;
[20](https://docs.rs#20)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)pub mod sync;
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)pub use map::{FrozenBTreeMap, FrozenMap};
[24](https://docs.rs#24)pub use vec::FrozenVec;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)
[26](https://docs.rs#26)#[cfg(feature = "indexmap")]
[27](https://docs.rs#27)pub use index_map::FrozenIndexMap;
[28](https://docs.rs#28)#[cfg(feature = "indexmap")]
[29](https://docs.rs#29)pub use index_set::FrozenIndexSet;

Returns a reference to the value corresponding to the key.

The key may be any borrowed form of the map’s key type, but
[ Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) and

[on the borrowed form](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html)

`Eq`*must*match those for the key type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use elsa::FrozenBTreeMap;
let map = FrozenBTreeMap::new();
map.insert(1, Box::new("a"));
assert_eq!(map.get(&1), Some(&"a"));
assert_eq!(map.get(&2), None);
```
Applies a function to the owner of the value corresponding to the key (if any).

The key may be any borrowed form of the map’s key type, but
[ Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) and

[on the borrowed form](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html)

`Eq`*must*match those for the key type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use elsa::FrozenBTreeMap;
let map = FrozenBTreeMap::new();
map.insert(1, Box::new("a"));
assert_eq!(map.map_get(&1, Clone::clone), Some(Box::new("a")));
assert_eq!(map.map_get(&2, Clone::clone), None);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/elsa/map.rs.html#453-455)

#### pub fn [into_tuple_vec](https://docs.rs#method.into_tuple_vec)(self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[(K, V)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)>

Collects the contents of this map into a vector of tuples.

The order of the entries is as if iterating a [ BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html) (ordered by key).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use elsa::FrozenBTreeMap;
let map = FrozenBTreeMap::new();
map.insert(1, Box::new("a"));
map.insert(2, Box::new("b"));
let mut tuple_vec = map.into_tuple_vec();
tuple_vec.sort();
assert_eq!(tuple_vec, vec![(1, Box::new("a")), (2, Box::new("b"))]);
```

Returns a reference to the key and value matching a borrowed key.

The key argument may be any borrowed form of the map’s key type,
but [ Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) and

[on the borrowed form](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html)

`Eq`*must*match those for the key type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use elsa::FrozenMap;
let map = FrozenMap::new();
map.insert(Box::new("1"), Box::new("a"));
assert_eq!(map.get_key_value(&"1"), Some((&"1", &"a")));
assert_eq!(map.get_key_value(&"2"), None);
```

### impl<K: [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html) + [Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html), V: [StableDeref](https://docs.rs/stable_deref_trait/1.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stable_deref_trait/trait.StableDeref.html), S: [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)> [FrozenIndexMap](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenIndexMap.html)<K, V, S>

If the key exists in the map, returns a reference to the corresponding value, otherwise inserts a new entry in the map for that key and returns a reference to the generated value.

Existing values are never overwritten.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use elsa::index_map::FrozenIndexMap;
let map = FrozenIndexMap::new();
assert_eq!(map.insert(1, Box::new("a")), &"a");
assert_eq!(map.insert(1, Box::new("b")), &"a");
```

#### pub fn [insert_full](https://docs.rs#method.insert_full)(&self, k: K, v: V) -> ([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), &V::[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target))

If the key exists in the map, returns a reference to the corresponding value and its index, otherwise inserts a new entry in the map for that key and returns a reference to the generated value and its index.

Existing values are never overwritten.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use elsa::index_map::FrozenIndexMap;

assert_eq!(map.insert_full(12, Box::new("a")), (0, &"a"));
assert_eq!(map.insert_full(12, Box::new("b")), (0, &"a"));
```

Returns a reference to the key-value mapping corresponding to an index.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use elsa::index_map::FrozenIndexMap;
let map = FrozenIndexMap::new();
let (idx, _ref) = map.insert_full(Box::new("foo"), Box::new("a"));
assert_eq!(idx, 0);
assert_eq!(map.get_index(idx), Some((&"foo", &"a")));
assert_eq!(map.get_index(idx + 1), None);
```
Returns a reference to the key, along with its index and a reference to its value

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments-2)Arguments

- `k`may be any type that implements- `Equivalent<K>`

```
use elsa::index_map::FrozenIndexMap;
let map = FrozenIndexMap::new();
map.insert("1", Box::new("a"));
assert_eq!(map.get_full("1"), Some((0, "1", &"a")));
assert_eq!(map.get_full("2"), None);
```

Collects the contents of this map into a vector of tuples.

The order of the entries is as if iterating an [ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/indexmap/map/struct.IndexMap.html).

### impl<T: [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html) + [Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) + [StableDeref](https://docs.rs/stable_deref_trait/1.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stable_deref_trait/trait.StableDeref.html), S: [BuildHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)> [FrozenIndexSet](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenIndexSet.html)<T, S>

If the value exists in the set, returns a reference to the corresponding value, otherwise inserts a new entry in the set for that value and returns a reference to it.

Existing values are never overwritten.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use elsa::index_set::FrozenIndexSet;
let set = FrozenIndexSet::new();
let a_ref = set.insert(Box::new("a"));
let aa = "a";
let other_a_ref = unsafe { aa.as_ptr() as *const &str};
let other_a = Box::new(aa);
assert!(!std::ptr::eq(a_ref, other_a_ref));
assert!(std::ptr::eq(a_ref, set.insert(other_a)));
```

# elsa::sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/elsa/1.11.2/elsa/sync/index.html

## Expand description

**This module is experimental**

This module provides threadsafe versions of FrozenMap and FrozenVec, ideal for use as a cache.

These lock internally, however locks only last as long as the method calls

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FrozenB](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenBTreeMap.html)- Tree - Map
- Append-only threadsafe version of `std::collections::BTreeMap`where insertion does not require mutable access
- [Frozen](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenMap.html)- Map
- Append-only threadsafe version of `std::collections::HashMap`where insertion does not require mutable access
- [Frozen](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenVec.html)- Vec
- Append-only threadsafe version of `std::vec::Vec`where insertion does not require mutable access
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator over FrozenVec, obtained via `.iter()`
- [Lock](https://docs.rs/struct.LockFreeFrozenVec.html)- Free - Frozen - Vec
- Append-only threadsafe version of `std::vec::Vec`where insertion does not require mutable access. Does not lock for reading, only allows`Copy`types and will spinlock on pushes without affecting reads. Note that this data structure is`34`pointers large on 64 bit systems, in contrast to`Vec`which is`3`pointers large.

# elsa - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/elsa/latest/elsa/

## Expand description

*🎵 Immutability never bothered me anyway 🎶*

This crate provides various “Frozen” collections.

These are append-only collections where references to entries can be held
on to even across insertions. This is safe because these collections only
support storing data that’s present behind some indirection – i.e. `String`,
`Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, etc, and they only yield references to the data behind the
allocation (`&str`, `&[T]`, and `&T` respectively)

The typical use case is having a global cache of strings or other data which the rest of the program borrows from.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use map::`- [FrozenBTreeMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.FrozenBTreeMap.html);
- `pub use map::`- [FrozenMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.FrozenMap.html);
- `pub use vec::`- [FrozenVec](https://docs.rs/vec/struct.FrozenVec.html);
- `pub use index_map::`- [FrozenIndexMap](https://docs.rs/index_map/struct.FrozenIndexMap.html);
- `pub use index_set::`- [FrozenIndexSet](https://docs.rs/index_set/struct.FrozenIndexSet.html);

---

# elsa 1.11.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/elsa/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

---

# indexmap 2.14.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/indexmap/^2.0.2

# indexmap

A pure-Rust hash table which preserves (in a limited sense) insertion order.

This crate implements compact map and set data-structures, where the iteration order of the keys is independent from their hash or value. It preserves insertion order (except after removals), and it allows lookup of entries by either hash table key or numerical index.

Note: this crate was originally released under the name `ordermap`,
but it was renamed to `indexmap` to better reflect its features.
The [ ordermap](https://crates.io/crates/ordermap) crate now exists
as a wrapper over

`indexmap` with stronger ordering properties.# Background

This was inspired by Python 3.6's new dict implementation (which remembers the insertion order and is fast to iterate, and is compact in memory).

Some of those features were translated to Rust, and some were not. The result was indexmap, a hash table that has following properties:

- Order is **independent of hash function**and hash values of keys.
- Fast to iterate.
- Indexed in compact space.
- Preserves insertion order **as long**as you don't call`.remove()`,`.swap_remove()`, or other methods that explicitly change order. The alternate`.shift_remove()`does preserve relative order.
- Uses hashbrown for the inner table, just like Rust's libstd `HashMap`does.

## Performance

`IndexMap` derives a couple of performance facts directly from how it is constructed,
which is roughly:

A raw hash table of key-value indices, and a vector of key-value pairs.

-
Iteration is very fast since it is on the dense key-values.
-
Removal is fast since it moves memory areas only in the table, and uses a single swap in the vector.
-
Lookup is fast-ish because the initial 7-bit hash lookup uses SIMD, and indices are densely stored. Lookup also is slow-ish since the actual key-value pairs are stored separately. (Visible when cpu caches size is limiting.)
-
In practice, `IndexMap`has been tested out as the hashmap in rustc in[PR45282](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/45282)and the performance was roughly on par across the whole workload.
-
If you want the properties of `IndexMap`, or its strongest performance points fits your workload, it might be the best hash table implementation.

# Recent Changes

See [RELEASES.md](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/indexmap/blob/main/RELEASES.md).

---

# stable_deref_trait 1.2.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stable_deref_trait/^1.1.1

This crate defines an unsafe marker trait, StableDeref, for container types which deref to a fixed address which is valid even when the containing type is moved. For example, Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String implement this trait. Additionally, it defines CloneStableDeref for types like Rc where clones deref to the same address.

It is intended to be used by crates such as [owning_ref](https://crates.io/crates/owning_ref) and [rental](https://crates.io/crates/rental), as well as library authors who wish to make their code interoperable with such crates. For example, if you write a custom Vec type, you can implement StableDeref, and then users will be able to use your custom Vec type together with owning_ref and rental.

no_std support can be enabled by disabling default features (specifically "std"). In this case, the trait will not be implemented for the std types mentioned above, but you can still use it for your own types.

Enable the "alloc" feature (with default-features disabled) to have this trait be implemented for the above types from the built-in `alloc` crate, specifically

- `alloc::boxed::Box`
- `alloc::vec::Vec`
- `alloc::rc::Rc`
- `alloc::arc::Arc`
- `alloc::string::String`

For example, this crate can be built with alloc support via the following command:
`cargo build --no-default-features --features alloc`

Or added as a `Cargo.toml` dependency as follows:

```
[dependencies.stable_deref_trait]
version = "<version>"
default-features = false
features = [ "alloc" ]
```

# elsa 1.11.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/elsa/1.11.0

## elsa

*🎵 Immutability never bothered me anyway 🎶*

This crate provides various "frozen" collections.

These are append-only collections where references to entries can be held on to even across insertions. This is safe because these collections only support storing data that's present behind some indirection -- i.e. `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, etc, and they only yield references to the data behind the allocation (`&str`, `&[T]`, and `&T` respectively)

The typical use case is having a global cache of strings or other data which the rest of the program borrows from.

### Running all examples

```
```

# indexmap 2.14.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/indexmap/2.14.0

# indexmap

A pure-Rust hash table which preserves (in a limited sense) insertion order.

This crate implements compact map and set data-structures, where the iteration order of the keys is independent from their hash or value. It preserves insertion order (except after removals), and it allows lookup of entries by either hash table key or numerical index.

Note: this crate was originally released under the name `ordermap`,
but it was renamed to `indexmap` to better reflect its features.
The [ ordermap](https://crates.io/crates/ordermap) crate now exists
as a wrapper over

`indexmap` with stronger ordering properties.# Background

This was inspired by Python 3.6's new dict implementation (which remembers the insertion order and is fast to iterate, and is compact in memory).

Some of those features were translated to Rust, and some were not. The result was indexmap, a hash table that has following properties:

- Order is **independent of hash function**and hash values of keys.
- Fast to iterate.
- Indexed in compact space.
- Preserves insertion order **as long**as you don't call`.remove()`,`.swap_remove()`, or other methods that explicitly change order. The alternate`.shift_remove()`does preserve relative order.
- Uses hashbrown for the inner table, just like Rust's libstd `HashMap`does.

## Performance

`IndexMap` derives a couple of performance facts directly from how it is constructed,
which is roughly:

A raw hash table of key-value indices, and a vector of key-value pairs.

-
Iteration is very fast since it is on the dense key-values.
-
Removal is fast since it moves memory areas only in the table, and uses a single swap in the vector.
-
Lookup is fast-ish because the initial 7-bit hash lookup uses SIMD, and indices are densely stored. Lookup also is slow-ish since the actual key-value pairs are stored separately. (Visible when cpu caches size is limiting.)
-
In practice, `IndexMap`has been tested out as the hashmap in rustc in[PR45282](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/45282)and the performance was roughly on par across the whole workload.
-
If you want the properties of `IndexMap`, or its strongest performance points fits your workload, it might be the best hash table implementation.

See [RELEASES.md](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/indexmap/blob/main/RELEASES.md).

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/^1.0/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

# borsh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/borsh/^1.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

[§](https://docs.rs#ecosystem-features)Ecosystem features

-
**std**- When enabled,`borsh`uses the standard library. Disabling this feature will result in building the crate in`no_std`environment.To carter such builds, Borsh offers `io``BorshSerialize``BorshDeserialize``io::Read`,`io::Write`and`io::Result`.When **std**feature is enabled, those items are re-exports of corresponding`std::io`items. Otherwise they are borsh-specific types which mimic behaviour of corresponding standard types.

[§](https://docs.rs#default-features)Default features

- **std**- enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

-
**derive**- Gates derive macros of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)traits.
-
**unstable__schema**- Gates[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)trait and its derive macro. Gates[schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)module. This feature requires**derive**to be enabled too.
-
**rc**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for`Rc<T>``Arc<T>``no_std`setting`Rc`/`Arc`are pulled from`alloc`crate. Serializing and deserializing these types does not preserve identity and may result in multiple copies of the same data. Be sure that this is what you want before enabling this feature.
-
**hashbrown**- Pulls in[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)when no`std`is available. This feature is set to be mutually exclusive with**std**feature.
-
**bytes**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[Bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.Bytes.html)and[BytesMut](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.BytesMut.html). In`no_std`builds this keeps`bytes`in`no_std`mode; when**std**is enabled,`bytes/std`is enabled as well.
-
**bson**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[ObjectId](https://docs.rs/bson/2.9.0/bson/oid/struct.ObjectId.html).
-
**indexmap**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[indexmap::IndexMap](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/map/struct.IndexMap.html)and[IndexSet](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/set/struct.IndexSet.html)
-
**ascii**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html),[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for types from[ascii](https://docs.rs/ascii/1.1.0/ascii/)crate.
-
**de_strict_order**- Enables check that keys, parsed during deserialization of[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)and[BTreeSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/set/struct.BTreeSet.html)/[BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html)are encountered in ascending order with respect to[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)for hash collections, and[Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html)for btree ones. Deserialization emits error otherwise.If this feature is not enabled, it is possible that two different byte slices could deserialize into the same `HashMap`/`HashSet`object.

[§](https://docs.rs#config-aliases)Config aliases

- **hash_collections**- This is a feature alias, set up in- `build.rs`to be equivalent to (- **std**OR- **hashbrown**). # equivalent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/equivalent/^1.0/

## Expand description

[ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[are traits for key comparison in maps.](https://docs.rs/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`These may be used in the implementation of maps where the lookup type `Q`
may be different than the stored key type `K`.

- `Q: Equivalent<K>`checks for equality, similar to the- `HashMap<K, V>`constraint- `K: Borrow<Q>, Q: Eq`.
- `Q: Comparable<K>`checks the ordering, similar to the- `BTreeMap<K, V>`constraint- `K: Borrow<Q>, Q: Ord`.

These traits are not used by the maps in the standard library, but they may
add more flexibility in third-party map implementations, especially in
situations where a strict `K: Borrow<Q>` relationship is not available.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use equivalent::*;
use std::cmp::Ordering;
pub struct Pair<A, B>(pub A, pub B);
impl<'a, A: ?Sized, B: ?Sized, C, D> Equivalent<(C, D)> for Pair<&'a A, &'a B>
where
    A: Equivalent<C>,
    B: Equivalent<D>,
{
    fn equivalent(&self, key: &(C, D)) -> bool {
        self.0.equivalent(&key.0) && self.1.equivalent(&key.1)
    }
}
impl<'a, A: ?Sized, B: ?Sized, C, D> Comparable<(C, D)> for Pair<&'a A, &'a B>
where
    A: Comparable<C>,
    B: Comparable<D>,
{
    fn compare(&self, key: &(C, D)) -> Ordering {
        match self.0.compare(&key.0) {
            Ordering::Equal => self.1.compare(&key.1),
            not_equal => not_equal,
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    let key = (String::from("foo"), String::from("bar"));
    let q1 = Pair("foo", "bar");
    let q2 = Pair("boo", "bar");
    let q3 = Pair("foo", "baz");
    assert!(q1.equivalent(&key));
    assert!(!q2.equivalent(&key));
    assert!(!q3.equivalent(&key));
    assert_eq!(q1.compare(&key), Ordering::Equal);
    assert_eq!(q2.compare(&key), Ordering::Less);
    assert_eq!(q3.compare(&key), Ordering::Greater);
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Comparable](https://docs.rs/trait.Comparable.html)
- Key ordering trait.
- [Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html)
- Key equivalence trait.

# hashbrown - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hashbrown/^0.17/

## Expand description

This crate is a Rust port of Google’s high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash
map, adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust’s standard `HashMap`
and `HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_map/index.html)- map
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_set/index.html)- set
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_table/index.html)- table
- A hash table implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHashBuilder.html)- Hash - Builder
- Default hash builder for the `S`type parameter of`HashMap``HashSet`
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHasher.html)- Hasher
- Default hasher for `HashMap``HashSet`
- [HashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.HashMap.html)
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [HashSet](https://docs.rs/struct.HashSet.html)
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/struct.HashTable.html)- Table
- Low-level hash table with explicit hashing.

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1.9/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

See `scope_fifo()`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/^1.0.220/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/^2/

## Expand description

Structured, streaming values.

`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
It’s well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).

Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
```
By default, `sval` doesn’t depend on Rust’s standard library or integrate with its collection types.
To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["std"]
```
`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["derive"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-value-trait)The `Value` trait

[ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Value.html) is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called

*streams*.

`Value` is like `serde`’s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserialize`.Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-stream-trait)The `Stream` trait

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# fastrand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrand/^2/

## Expand description

A simple and fast random number generator.

The implementation uses [Wyrand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash), a simple and fast
generator but **not** cryptographically secure.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Flip a coin:

```
if fastrand::bool() {
    println!("heads");
} else {
    println!("tails");
}
```
Generate a random `i32`:

`let num = fastrand::i32(..);`Choose a random element in an array:

```
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let i = fastrand::usize(..v.len());
let elem = v[i];
```
Sample values from an array with `O(n)` complexity (`n` is the length of array):

```
fastrand::choose_multiple([1, 4, 5], 2);
fastrand::choose_multiple(0..20, 12);
```
Shuffle an array:

```
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
fastrand::shuffle(&mut v);
```
Generate a random [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) or

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let v: Vec<i32> = repeat_with(|| fastrand::i32(..)).take(10).collect();
let s: String = repeat_with(fastrand::alphanumeric).take(10).collect();
```
To get reproducible results on every run, initialize the generator with a seed:

```
// Pick an arbitrary number as seed.
fastrand::seed(7);
// Now this prints the same number on every run:
println!("{}", fastrand::u32(..));
```
To be more efficient, create a new [ Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html) instance instead of using the thread-local
generator:

```
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let mut rng = fastrand::Rng::new();
let mut bytes: Vec<u8> = repeat_with(|| rng.u8(..)).take(10_000).collect();
```
This crate aims to expose a core set of useful randomness primitives. For more niche algorithms,
consider using the [ fastrand-contrib](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand-contrib) crate alongside this one.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `std`(enabled by default): Enables the- `std`library. This is required for the global generator and global entropy. Without this feature,- `Rng`- `with_seed`
- `js`: Assumes that WebAssembly targets are being run in a JavaScript environment. See the- [WebAssembly Notes](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)section for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)WebAssembly Notes

For non-WASI WASM targets, there is additional subtlety to consider when utilizing the global RNG.
By default, `std` targets will use entropy sources in the standard library to seed the global RNG.
However, these sources are not available by default on WASM targets outside of WASI.

If the `js` feature is enabled, this crate will assume that it is running in a JavaScript
environment. At this point, the [ getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom) crate will be used in order to access the available
entropy sources and seed the global RNG. If the

`js` feature is not enabled, the global RNG will
use a predefined seed.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html)
- A random number generator.

# fnv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fnv/^1.0/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Fowler–Noll–Vo hash function](http://www.isthe.com/chongo/tech/comp/fnv/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

The FNV hash function is a custom `Hasher` implementation that is more
efficient for smaller hash keys.

[The Rust FAQ states that](https://www.rust-lang.org/en-US/faq.html#why-are-rusts-hashmaps-slow) while the default `Hasher` implementation,
SipHash, is good in many cases, it is notably slower than other algorithms
with short keys, such as when you have a map of integers to other values.
In cases like these, [FNV is demonstrably faster](https://cglab.ca/~abeinges/blah/hash-rs/).

Its disadvantages are that it performs badly on larger inputs, and provides no protection against collision attacks, where a malicious user can craft specific keys designed to slow a hasher down. Thus, it is important to profile your program to ensure that you are using small hash keys, and be certain that your program could not be exposed to malicious inputs (including being a networked server).

The Rust compiler itself uses FNV, as it is not worried about denial-of-service attacks, and can assume that its inputs are going to be small—a perfect use case for FNV.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-fnv-in-a-hashmap)Using FNV in a `HashMap`

The `FnvHashMap` type alias is the easiest way to use the standard library’s
`HashMap` with FNV.

```
use fnv::FnvHashMap;
let mut map = FnvHashMap::default();
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
map = FnvHashMap::with_capacity_and_hasher(10, Default::default());
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
```
Note, the standard library’s `HashMap::new` and `HashMap::with_capacity`
are only implemented for the `RandomState` hasher, so using `Default` to
get the hasher is the next best option.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-fnv-in-a-hashset)Using FNV in a `HashSet`

Similarly, `FnvHashSet` is a type alias for the standard library’s `HashSet`
with FNV.

```
use fnv::FnvHashSet;
let mut set = FnvHashSet::default();
set.insert(1);
set.insert(2);
set = FnvHashSet::with_capacity_and_hasher(10, Default::default());
set.insert(1);
set.insert(2);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FnvHasher](https://docs.rs/struct.FnvHasher.html)
- An implementation of the Fowler–Noll–Vo hash function.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [FnvBuild](https://docs.rs/type.FnvBuildHasher.html)- Hasher
- A builder for default FNV hashers.
- [FnvHash](https://docs.rs/type.FnvHashMap.html)- Map
- A `HashMap`using a default FNV hasher.
- [FnvHash](https://docs.rs/type.FnvHashSet.html)- Set
- A `HashSet`using a default FNV hasher.

# itertools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/itertools/^0.14/

## Expand description

Extra iterator adaptors, functions and macros.

To extend [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with methods in this crate, import
the

[trait:](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html)

`Itertools``use itertools::Itertools;`Now, new methods like [ interleave](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html#method.interleave)
are available on all iterators:

```
use itertools::Itertools;
let it = (1..3).interleave(vec![-1, -2]);
itertools::assert_equal(it, vec![1, -1, 2, -2]);
```
Most iterator methods are also provided as functions (with the benefit
that they convert parameters using [ IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)):

```
use itertools::interleave;
for elt in interleave(&[1, 2, 3], &[2, 3, 4]) {
    /* loop body */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

- `use_std`- Enabled by default.
- Disable to compile itertools using `#![no_std]`. This disables any item that depend on allocations (see the`use_alloc`feature) and hash maps (like`unique`,`counts`,`into_grouping_map`and more).

- `use_alloc`- Enabled by default.
- Enables any item that depend on allocations (like `chunk_by`,`kmerge`,`join`and many more).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of itertools requires Rust 1.63.0 or later.

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.1/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.220/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/indexmap/2.14.0/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/indexmap/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `quickcheck`: Adds implementations for the- `quickcheck::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `borsh`(- **deprecated**): Adds implementations for- `BorshSerialize`- `BorshDeserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `borsh`- `indexmap`,- `borsh v1.5.6`added an- `indexmap`feature that should be used instead of enabling the feature here.

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- `IndexMap`
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- A hash set implemented using `IndexMap`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [indexmap](https://docs.rs/macro.indexmap.html)- `std`
- Create an `IndexMap`
- [indexmap_](https://docs.rs/macro.indexmap_with_default.html)- with_ - default
- Create an `IndexMap``BuildHasherDefault`
- [indexset](https://docs.rs/macro.indexset.html)- `std`
- Create an `IndexSet`
- [indexset_](https://docs.rs/macro.indexset_with_default.html)- with_ - default
- Create an `IndexSet``BuildHasherDefault`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [TryReserve](https://docs.rs/struct.TryReserveError.html)- Error
- The error type for `try_reserve`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [GetDisjoint](https://docs.rs/enum.GetDisjointMutError.html)- MutError
- The error type returned by `get_disjoint_indices_mut`

- [Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html)
- Key equivalence trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/indexmap/2.14.0/target-redirect/indexmap/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `quickcheck`: Adds implementations for the- `quickcheck::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `borsh`(- **deprecated**): Adds implementations for- `BorshSerialize`- `BorshDeserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `borsh`- `indexmap`,- `borsh v1.5.6`added an- `indexmap`feature that should be used instead of enabling the feature here.

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`

# Equivalent in indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/indexmap/^2.0.2/trait.Equivalent.html

```
pub trait Equivalent<K>{
    // Required method
    fn
```
[equivalent](https://docs.rs#tymethod.equivalent)(&self, key: [&K](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html);
}## Expand description

Key equivalence trait.

This trait allows hash table lookup to be customized. It has one blanket
implementation that uses the regular solution with `Borrow` and `Eq`, just
like `HashMap` does, so that you can pass `&str` to lookup into a map with
`String` keys and so on.

[§](https://docs.rs#contract)Contract

The implementor **must** hash like `K`, if it is hashable.

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Rc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Rc` each time the `Rc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

# Deserialize in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
